extracted.intended_audience: general readers and young persons seeking practical moral self-improvement (e.g., aspiring virtuous citizens, young printers, and self-educating youths)
extracted.subtask_description: Benjamin Franklin's practical regimen for acquiring moral virtues: a list of thirteen named virtues with short precepts, an ordered schedule for practicing them, a daily/weekly self-examination ledger, a 24-hour time scheme, and related social/editorial recommendations. The guidance is both prescriptive (how to practice) and evaluative (what counts as success/failure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance
rubrics_metrics.description: Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placed first because temperance procures coolness and clearness of head necessary for constant vigilance; devote the first week's strict attention to avoiding every offence against Temperance and mark faults nightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second virtue to facilitate gaining knowledge (listen more than speak); intended to break habits of prattling, punning, and joking that attract trifling company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a specific 24-hour 'scheme of employment' scheduling rise, study, work, meals, examination of the day, sleep, etc.; acknowledged as difficult for those (like masters) who must receive business at varying hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to sustain firm adherence to the other virtues once acquired; made a central habit to maintain subsequent practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality
rubrics_metrics.description: Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; i.e., waste nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frugality (with Industry) is credited with producing early easiness of circumstances, affluence, and independence enabling practice of other virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes acquisition of fortune and useful standing; paired with Frugality as means to secure independence from debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly, and, if you speak, speak accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports trust and reputation; linked to gaining confidence of country and being entrusted with public employ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong none by doing injuries, or omitting the benefits that are your duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as a civic duty; contributing to public confidence and honorable employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extreams; forbear resenting injuries so much as you think they deserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to temper emotional excesses and keep relations pleasant; positioned among virtues that follow Frugality and Industry in the sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolerate no uncleanliness in body, cloaths, or habitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical virtue for personal and domestic order; part of the catalogue of concrete, actionable behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be not disturbed at trifles, or at accidents common or unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages emotional steadiness; listed to prevent needless perturbation over ordinary occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chastity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely use venery but for health or offspring, never to dulness, weakness, or the injury of your own or another's peace or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives clear limits on sexual conduct tied to health and reputation; acknowledges moderation rather than absolute abstinence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitate Jesus and Socrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Added after being informed of pride; practical rules include forbidding dogmatic words (certainly, undoubtedly), avoiding direct contradiction, proposing opinions modestly (I conceive, I apprehend), and answering opponents by conceding where applicable — all to make conversation more pleasant and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of self-examination (ledger and marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A little book with a page for each virtue; each page has seven columns (one per day) and thirteen red lines (one per virtue) where faults are marked by a little black spot in the day's column and virtue's row.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to record nightly faults; originally written on paper then transferred to ivory leaves with red-ink lines and black-lead marks that can be wiped out; the marks visually show progress as lines clear of spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly focus progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a week's strict attention to each virtue successively: first week Temperance alone, then add Silence the second week, proceed cumulatively until all thirteen are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete course is 13 weeks; repeating courses (four per year originally) builds habit by focusing attention without distraction and permits seeing progressive improvement on the ledger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of virtues for acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange virtues in an order so acquisition of earlier ones facilitates later ones (Temperance first, then Silence, then Order, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance chosen first to secure clarity of mind, Silence next to enable learning by listening, Order to free time for study; Brad/sequence rationale spelled out to optimize habit formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prayers/mottos to support practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefix the tables of examination with brief prayers and mottoes soliciting divine assistance to increase wisdom and strengthen resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include short prayers to 'Powerful Goodness' and lines from poets/Scripture; presented as a moral and psychological aid to sustain the regimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily 24-hour scheme of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed schedule allocating hours for rising, washing, contriving day's business, study, work, reading/overlooking accounts, dinner, putting things in place, supper/diversion, examination of the day, and sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part of the day linked to reflective 'What good shall I do this day?' and 'What good have I done to-day?' questions; the scheme operationalizes the virtue of Order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints and realistic adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize some virtues (Order) may be impracticable for masters with irregular business; adjust expectations rather than strict observance in such cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin notes difficulty with Order due to business calls and personal habits; he recommends continuing effort but accepts partial progress and realistic modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sectarian content in general moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude distinguishing tenets of any particular sect from a method for virtue so it can be acceptable across religions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin purposely avoided sectarian specifics to ensure the method would not prejudice adherents of any religion against it, aiming for universal applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for founding a Society of Virtue (membership & secrecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should declare assent to a simple creed and have exercised themselves with the thirteen weeks' examination and practice; society spread initially among young single men; keep existence secret until considerable to avoid improper solicitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members should search for ingenuous, well-disposed youths to initiate; members to afford advice and mutual assistance in promoting each other's interests; constitution and name ('The Society of the Free and Easy') proposed; rationale: form virtuous citizens and promote unanimity to good rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core creed for universal moral society
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise creed: there is one God who made all things; He governs the world by providence; He ought to be worshiped by adoration, prayer, thanksgiving; the most acceptable service of God is doing good to man; the soul is immortal; God will reward virtue and punish vice either here or hereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as essentials common to known religions and intentionally free of divisive particulars; required assent for Society membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial ethics for printers/newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Refuse to print libel, personal abuse, or private altercation in newspapers; if an author insists, print separately for him to distribute, but do not pollute the paper with private detraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin describes contractual obligation to subscribers to provide useful and entertaining content, and that printing scurrilous reflections harms the public and may have pernicious political consequences; he encourages printers to decline such pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for female education in accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach young females bookkeeping and accounts rather than focusing solely on music or dancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: practical value in widowhood for preserving assets, avoiding imposition, and enabling them to continue a profitable house or business until a son can take over; suggested as socially useful education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations for public preaching (authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preachers should avoid passing off others' writings or published works as their own; authenticity matters to maintain trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of a preacher (Hemphill) whose popularity collapsed after detection of quoted material; Franklin preferred good sermons made by others to bad originals but recognized the reputational risk of unattributed borrowing.
